Using ALS samples only and fitting covariate-adjusted continuous models separately for each spinal-cord region, the strongest gene-level associations with disease duration were found in the cervical spinal cord.

The single strongest negative correlate of longer disease duration was CHIT1 (beta = -0.301 per year, t = -6.78, FDR = 1.5e-05), followed by CD37, APOC2, HAVCR2, NCF2, HLA-DMB, SLC29A1, ARL11, GPX1, and UNC93B1. These genes were lower in longer-duration ALS cases and many belong to myeloid / inflammatory programs.

The strongest positive correlates of longer disease duration in cervical cord were IGLC2 and TTN, followed by AC136475.3 and AC245041.2.

Lumbar and thoracic cord showed directionally similar nominal negative associations for genes such as CHIT1 and APOC2, but no gene survived FDR correction there, so the most robust answer is cervical-centered.

Therefore, the best-supported individual genes showing the strongest correlation with ALS disease duration are: CHIT1 (strongest overall, negative), CD37, APOC2, HAVCR2, NCF2, HLA-DMB, SLC29A1, ARL11, GPX1, UNC93B1 on the negative side, and IGLC2 plus TTN on the positive side, with the evidence strongest in cervical spinal cord.
